evidence_quotes.quote: The review methodology is based on a three-step article search, selection, and content review process.
Another JMA, the Waikato River Settlement of 2010, places New Zealand’s longest river under a co-management model by the Crown and the Maori people (Aho, 2009).

Compared to the challenges and conflicts around competing water uses and water resources management, there is far less attention paid in the literature to the challenges related to the provision of water services to indigenous populations.

The issue of payments can be especially controversial with indigenous communities (Pearce, Willis, & Jenkin, 2007). Apart from the actual hardship and difficulties in producing the payment, the cultural perception of water as a ‘gift of Nature’ tends to make the acceptance of a tariff system difficult.

The available research on sanitation and hygiene in relation to indigenous peoples consists mainly of studies on the incidence of different diseases, in turn relating these to sanitation and hygiene as environmental factors.

This review of the published peer-reviewed literature on water and indigenous peoples finds the greatest share of research to focus on issues of water and environmental resources rather than WaSH (water, sanitation and hygiene) practices or services, and mostly on high-income countries.

criterion_notes.c1: Yes (partially): although 132 of the 185 reviewed articles concern water resources, spiritual values, conflicts, rights, and planning, the review explicitly covers 'Water as a basic service' (13 papers) and 'Hygiene and sanitation' (40 papers) among indigenous peoples.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses legal, institutional, and governance topics ('Legislative frameworks and indigenous rights', collaborative river co-management, participatory planning, rural community management, and intercultural dialogue), so it would pass Criterion 2 in isolation (though plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because the paper fails Criteria 3, 4, and 5). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no': the legislative and governance analysis focuses on natural-resource and river-basin water rights (e.g., UNDRIP, Native Title Act, New Zealand Resource Management Act and Waikato River joint management agreements, US Winters doctrine), Australian 'shared responsibility agreements' involve behavioural hygiene promotion, and the WaSH basic-services section only briefly notes in two sentences that indigenous cultural views of water as a gift of Nature make acceptance of tariffs controversial (citing one attitude study, Pearce et al., 2007) alongside calls for culturally adapted project delivery and intercultural dialogue, rather than analyzing any rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: No: the article contains no primary empirical data and is a broad scoping/narrative thematic overview of 185 Scopus-indexed papers (reporting only topic counts in Table 1 and narrative summaries of research themes and gaps) rather than a systematic empirical synthesis with study-level extraction, methodological appraisal, or empirical synthesis of exposure-outcome relationships.
criterion_notes.c4: No: beyond general background statements in the Introduction that indigenous groups have lower service coverage, the Results report thematic article counts and high-level narrative summaries (noting that sanitation/hygiene studies mainly examine parasitic/infectious disease incidence) without synthesizing empirical household or community outcomes on access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: No: while the review's bibliographic search procedure is described, study-level populations/units of analysis, specific legal/governance exposures governing service access, and corresponding service-access outcomes cannot be identified from the narrative overview.

study_design: Narrative/scoping thematic literature review (keyword search in Scopus yielding 185 articles grouped by topic)
country: Global / multi-country (literature review predominantly covering the US, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia, with additional studies from Latin America, Asia, and Africa)
population_and_sample: 185 peer-reviewed articles selected from 782 Scopus records on indigenous peoples, ethnic minorities, or aboriginal populations and water, sanitation, and hygiene (no primary empirical sample)
exposure: Broad thematic literature topics (spiritual values, resource conflicts, river/basin water rights and co-management, participatory basin planning, traditional ecological knowledge, behavioural hygiene agreements, and cultural attitudes toward water payments); no specific service-access legal/administrative exposure empirically synthesized
outcome: Thematic article counts across six topic areas (Table 1) and narrative summary of literature themes and research gaps; no empirical water or sanitation service-access outcome synthesized
rationale: Excluded as E05 (no primary empirical evidence and not a systematic empirical synthesis of governance-to-access evidence). Jiménez, Cortobius, and Kjellén (2014) conduct a broad scoping/thematic literature review of 185 Scopus articles on indigenous peoples and water, grouping papers into six topic counts (Table 1) and providing a narrative overview without study-level data extraction, quality assessment, or empirical synthesis of exposures and service-access outcomes (failing Criteria 3, 4, and 5, so plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude'). Furthermore, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, its legal and institutional discussion focuses on natural-resource and river-basin water rights and co-management, behavioural hygiene promotion ('shared responsibility agreements'), general intercultural project delivery, and a brief two-sentence mention of cultural resistance to paying for water, rather than analyzing a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
